items.mnemonic_text: A nose pointing at oneself: 'me', self.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The staring <radical>eye</radical> that watches everything finally gets curious about itself. It swivels all the way around until it's pressed right up against a cracked mirror in Sei's school bathroom, pupil to pupil with its own reflection — recognizing, for the very first time, itself.
items.reading_mnemonic: Still at that mirror, a boy named <reading>Jeeves</reading> catches his own stare looking back and mutters <reading>じ</reading> — jeez — mortified that of everyone in the school, he's the one caught staring at himself.
items.description: 自 opens with a short diagonal tick above the top-left corner of the box — a stroke that 目 simply doesn't have; 目 is a plain, evenly-ruled rectangle with two level bars inside. 白 carries that same top tick, but its box is shorter and squarer with only a single centered bar, reading flatter and more compact than 自's taller, narrower frame.

example_sentences.japanese: 週末は自由です。
example_sentences.english: The weekend is free.
example_sentences.furigana: 週[しゅう]末[まつ]は自[じ]由[ゆう]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 自転車で公園へ行きます。
example_sentences.english: I go to the park by bicycle.
example_sentences.furigana: 自[じ]転[てん]車[しゃ]で公[こう]園[えん]へ行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 山の自然はきれいです。
example_sentences.english: The mountain's nature is beautiful.
example_sentences.furigana: 山[やま]の自[し]然[ぜん]はきれいです。

items.mnemonic_text: An altar (示) marking earth (土): a shrine, and by extension a company.
items.meaning_mnemonic: On orientation day, the new hires drive the <radical>earth</radical> signpost into the ground behind Grandma Kane's shrine, right beside the stone <radical>altar</radical> where offerings sit out for everyone to see. Stake in the soil, altar in front of it — that's a company: a group planted on its own ground, showing itself off to the world.
items.reading_mnemonic: Still behind the shrine, a new hire named <reading>Shae</reading> trips over the freshly staked signpost and yelps <reading>しゃ</reading> as she stumbles face-first into the altar's offering tray — her first day at the company already the stuff of legend.
items.description: 社 originally named the local earth god's shrine — the altar raised on a patch of claimed ground for a village's protector spirit. The word later stretched to cover any group organized around a shared institution, which is why it equally means a shrine and a company: the modern sense kept the idea of a formal body bound to a place, not the religious content.

example_sentences.japanese: 父は会社で働いています。
example_sentences.english: My father works at a company.
example_sentences.furigana: 父[ちち]は会[かい]社[しゃ]で働[はたら]いています。

example_sentences.japanese: 姉は新聞社で働いています。
example_sentences.english: My older sister works at a newspaper company.
example_sentences.furigana: 姉[あね]は新[しん]聞[ぶん]社[しゃ]で働[はたら]いています。

example_sentences.japanese: 社長はいつも忙しいです。
example_sentences.english: The company president is always busy.
example_sentences.furigana: 社[しゃ]長[ちょう]はいつも忙[いそが]しいです。

items.mnemonic_text: An old man bent over a stick: a person.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Every day, the same stooped shuffle you know as <radical>old</radical> reappears at the crosswalk just as the sun climbs behind that little barred window marking a new <radical>day</radical>, and traffic idles while it crosses. Rain or shine, that shuffle is the one figure the neighborhood recognizes — not by name, just as a person who shows up every day.
items.reading_mnemonic: The driver stuck idling at that crosswalk, a man named <reading>Shuji</reading>, finally leans on his horn and shouts <reading>しゃ</reading> — shoo! — at the shuffling old figure, who doesn't even glance up before finishing the crossing at exactly the same pace.
items.description: 者 almost never stands alone as a word; it works as a suffix stitched onto a verb or field to name whoever does it, much the way English -er turns 'teach' into 'teacher'. Learning it as a floating idea of a person is the right starting point, but expect to meet it glued onto the end of something else far more often than by itself.

example_sentences.japanese: 私の母は医者です。
example_sentences.english: My mother is a doctor.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]の母[はは]は医[い]者[しゃ]です。

example_sentences.japanese: あの学者は有名です。
example_sentences.english: That scholar is famous.
example_sentences.furigana: あの学[がく]者[しゃ]は有[ゆう]名[めい]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は科学者になりました。
example_sentences.english: He became a scientist.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は科[か]学[がく]者[しゃ]になりました。

items.mnemonic_text: A workbench stacked with tools: one's trade, business.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>sheep</radical> plants its four stiff legs on the level <radical>ground</radical> beneath a <radical>tree</radical>, hangs a little sign off a low branch, and spends the whole day there chewing calmly through paperwork, unbothered and punctual, running its own steady little trade. This is the sheep's business.
items.reading_mnemonic: Every morning a regular customer named <reading>Geo</reading> strolls up to the sheep's stand under the tree, and the sheep bleats <reading>ぎょう</reading> back at him like a receipt stamping shut — same tree, same ground, same bleat, business as usual.

example_sentences.japanese: 授業の前に宿題をしました。
example_sentences.english: I did my homework before class.
example_sentences.furigana: 授[じゅ]業[ぎょう]の前[まえ]に宿[しゅく]題[だい]をしました。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女は来年大学を卒業します。
example_sentences.english: She's graduating from university next year.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]は来[らい]年[ねん]大[だい]学[がく]を卒[そつ]業[ぎょう]します。

example_sentences.japanese: 今日、残業があります。
example_sentences.english: I have overtime today.
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]、残[ざん]業[ぎょう]があります。

items.mnemonic_text: A cloth over a stand where the city market gathers.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You stroll into the town square and above every stall hangs a bright piece of <radical>cloth</radical> on a rod, snapping in the wind. On the biggest stall a pot steams away, and the vendor keeps slamming the flat disc of its <radical>lid</radical> back down over the rim so nobody smells the stew for free. Rows of cloth and clanging lids stretch as far as you can see. This is the heart of the city, its bustling market.
items.reading_mnemonic: The busiest stall belongs to Shi, a sharp-eyed vendor who greets every shopper crossing the market with a cheerful 「<reading>し</reading>!」. Follow her voice and you'll always find the center of the city.
items.description: Means city or market; shows up in words for towns and municipal places like 市 (city) and city names.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は去年からこの市に住んでいます。
example_sentences.english: I've been living in this city since last year.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は去[きょ]年[ねん]からこの市[し]に住[す]んでいます。

example_sentences.japanese: 市の図書館は駅の隣にあります。
example_sentences.english: The city library is right next to the station.
example_sentences.furigana: 市[し]の図[と]書[しょ]館[かん]は駅[えき]の隣[となり]にあります。

example_sentences.japanese: 週末に市の公園を散歩しました。
example_sentences.english: I took a walk through the city park over the weekend.
example_sentences.furigana: 週[しゅう]末[まつ]に市[し]の公[こう]園[えん]を散[さん]歩[ぽ]しました。

items.mnemonic_text: A horse (馬) inspected all over (侴): to test, examine.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>horse</radical> gallops in, all boxy body and dust-kicking hooves, expecting a race. Instead a vet in a lab coat pins it to a scale, shines a light in its eyes, and checks its teeth one by one. The horse stamps and snorts, furious, but every inch of it gets examined before it's ever let out to run.
items.reading_mnemonic: Ken, the sword-collecting dog, guards the clinic door with a wall of antique blades gleaming behind him. Every time the horse tries to bolt past without finishing its checkup, Ken barks one sharp <reading>けん</reading> — <reading>Ken</reading> means nobody skips the exam.

example_sentences.japanese: 明日試験があります。
example_sentences.english: There's an exam tomorrow.
example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]試[し]験[けん]があります。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女は毎週実験をします。
example_sentences.english: She does an experiment every week.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]は毎[まい]週[しゅう]実[じっ]験[けん]をします。

example_sentences.japanese: 学生は図書館で試験を受けます。
example_sentences.english: The student takes the exam at the library.
example_sentences.furigana: 学[がく]生[せい]は図[と]書[しょ]館[かん]で試[し]験[けん]を受[う]けます。

items.mnemonic_text: A field (田) sitting over the heart (心): thoughts forming.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You stand at the edge of your flooded <radical>rice field</radical>, its paths crossing the plots into a grid below you. Above it your wounded <radical>heart</radical> drags itself up and hovers there, thumping, while you stare at the grid, turning the harvest over one square at a time. That thumping stillness is what it looks like to think.
items.reading_mnemonic: A heron named Shi stands dead still over the rice field, chewing over something enormous. Every few minutes it snaps its beak and lets out one flat <reading>し</reading> — proof that all that stillness is <reading>Shi</reading>'s thought, not sleep.

example_sentences.japanese: この本はどう思いますか。
example_sentences.english: What do you think of this book?
example_sentences.furigana: この本[ほん]はどう思[おも]いますか。

example_sentences.japanese: 私はそう思います。
example_sentences.english: I think so.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]はそう思[おも]います。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女は忙しいと思います。
example_sentences.english: I think she's busy.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]は忙[いそが]しいと思[おも]います。

items.mnemonic_text: A bow (弓) with its string pulled taut: to pull.
items.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, past the improbable vending machine, an archer plants their feet and hauls back on a springy <radical>bow</radical>, bending its stacked-curve wood taut until the string bites into their fingers. That single act of hauling back is the whole meaning: to pull.
items.reading_mnemonic: A parrot named Inko perches on the vending machine and screeches <reading>いん</reading> the instant the string snaps taut, like an <reading>inn</reading> bell ringing for a guest who arrived too fast. Every hiker on the trail flinches at the sound before they even see the arrow.

example_sentences.japanese: 引き出しの中に鍵があります。
example_sentences.english: There's a key inside the drawer.
example_sentences.furigana: 引[ひ]き出[だ]しの中[なか]に鍵[かぎ]があります。

example_sentences.japanese: 来月、家族で引っ越します。
example_sentences.english: Next month, my family and I are moving.
example_sentences.furigana: 来[らい]月[げつ]、家[か]族[ぞく]で引[ひ]っ越[こ]します。

example_sentences.japanese: 割引で靴を買いました。
example_sentences.english: I bought the shoes at a discount.
example_sentences.furigana: 割[わり]引[びき]で靴[くつ]を買[か]いました。

items.mnemonic_text: An arrow (矢) hitting the mouth's (口) point: to know for certain.
items.meaning_mnemonic: On Sei's sports field, an <radical>arrow</radical> streaks straight across the grass and thunks dead center into the target, and in that same instant your <radical>mouth</radical> snaps open with the answer — no hesitation, just the fact flying out as fast and true as the shot. That instant, certain hit is knowing something.
items.reading_mnemonic: Chibi the parrot roosts on that same target and shrieks <reading>ち</reading> the second the arrow lands, confirming the answer before you can even say it out loud — a sharp <reading>chee</reading> of certainty every time.

example_sentences.japanese: 私はその人を知りません。
example_sentences.english: I don't know that person.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]はその人[ひと]を知[し]りません。

example_sentences.japanese: 先生が私たちに知らせました。
example_sentences.english: The teacher let us know.
example_sentences.furigana: 先[せん]生[せい]が私[わたし]たちに知[し]らせました。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼はすぐに承知しました。
example_sentences.english: He agreed right away.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]はすぐに承[しょう]知[ち]しました。

items.mnemonic_text: Small (小) with a slash taken off: even fewer.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Take something <radical>small</radical> — that hook with two flanking dots — and slice one more dot away with a downward stroke. Now there's even less than small: barely anything left. When you take a bite out of small, what remains is few.
items.reading_mnemonic: Sho, the tiny stage magician, opens his white-gloved hand to reveal only a few crumbs of confetti — "<reading>しょう</reading> time!" he squeaks, and even the doves look unimpressed by how little there is. His whole act, like everything about him, is small and few.
items.description: 少 is 小 with one extra stroke: a slash sweeping down and to the left below the base. Take that tail away and you are back to 小.

example_sentences.japanese: 今日は少し寒いです。
example_sentences.english: It's a little cold today.
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]は少[すこ]し寒[さむ]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: この本は少し高いです。
example_sentences.english: This book is a little expensive.
example_sentences.furigana: この本[ほん]は少[すこ]し高[たか]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: 日本語を少し話します。
example_sentences.english: I speak a little Japanese.
example_sentences.furigana: 日本[にほん]語[ご]を少[すこ]し話[はな]します。

items.meaning_mnemonic: One stroke <radical>slides</radical> down from the top left across a bar of <radical>ground</radical>, and underneath it a <radical>right hand</radical> comes up to meet it. Two hands reaching in from opposite directions and closing on each other. Nobody is being paid for this and nobody is in charge of anybody. That is a <radical>friend</radical>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Yuu is the one who is always there before you, hand already out, drawing the greeting into a long two-beat call across the car park — 「<reading>ゆう</reading>」 — before you have even shut the car door. ゆう means somebody is glad to see you.

items.mnemonic_text: A road (辶) that splits away (韋): to differ.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A disembodied <radical>mouth</radical> plants itself at a fork in the road and bellows directions with total confidence, left, while your own footsteps quietly <radical>advance</radical> right instead, because the mouth's directions never match where the road goes. Two opinions, two paths: that is what it means to differ.
items.reading_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, a hiker named <reading>E</reading> takes the mouth's directions and immediately regrets it, stubbing her toe on a root and yelping <reading>い</reading>, which is exactly the sound of finding out, one more time, that the two of you always end up disagreeing.

example_sentences.japanese: テストで答えを間違えました。
example_sentences.english: I got the answer wrong on the test.
example_sentences.furigana: テストで答[こた]えを間[ま]違[ちが]えました。

example_sentences.japanese: この道は間違っています。
example_sentences.english: This is the wrong road.
example_sentences.furigana: この道[みち]は間違[まちが]っています。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女は電話番号を間違えました。
example_sentences.english: She got the phone number wrong.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]は電[でん]話[わ]番[ばん]号[ごう]を間[ま]違[ちが]えました。

items.mnemonic_text: A knife (刂) cutting a shape (另) apart: to separate.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The little rabbit is still buttering toast with its <radical>sword</radical> when a flexed <radical>power</radical>ful arm grabs the loaf and yanks, and a gaping <radical>mouth</radical> closes over half of it before the blade lands. Loaf ripped one way, sword swinging the other: one thing is now unmistakably two, kept separate.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank, someone waves off half a delivery, handing it to a woman named <reading>Betsy</reading> and calling out <reading>べつ</reading>: separate boat, separate load. The rabbit's loaf and its missing half drift downstream in different currents.

example_sentences.japanese: 今日は特別な料理を作りました。
example_sentences.english: Today I made a special dish.
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]は特[とく]別[べつ]な料[りょう]理[り]を作[つく]りました。

example_sentences.japanese: 私は別に忙しくないです。
example_sentences.english: I'm not particularly busy.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は別[べつ]に忙[いそが]しくないです。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は別の部屋にいます。
example_sentences.english: He's in a different room.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は別[べつ]の部屋[へや]にいます。

items.mnemonic_text: Big (大) with an extra drop of size: thick, fat.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a person standing with arms flung wide and legs spread in a huge X, filling the whole page. A single <radical>drop</radical> - a ladle of stew, not water - plops right onto his belly and soaks straight in. His stomach swells outward on the spot, arms pushed even wider by his own gut. That one dropped ladle is the difference between big and thick, fat.
items.reading_mnemonic: The cook who ladled that stew is a heavyset chef named <reading>Tai</reading>. He pats his own swollen belly, proud of the extra drop he added, and sighs <reading>たい</reading>, satisfied at how thick he's made himself.
items.description: 太 is 大 (big) with one extra dot. On 太 that dot sits low, tucked between the legs where the stew dripped in - the mark of something thickened. On 犬 (dog) the dot instead sits high, off the right arm, like a tail flicked up and out. Same big-person shape, different spot for the single drop.

example_sentences.japanese: 象の足はとても太い。
example_sentences.english: An elephant's legs are very thick.
example_sentences.furigana: 象[ぞう]の足[あし]はとても太[ふと]い。

example_sentences.japanese: 太陽は東から出る。

example_sentences.japanese: 蛇の体は太い。

example_sentences.furigana: 蛇[へび]の体[からだ]は太[ふと]い。

items.mnemonic_text: A cart's heavy load stacked high: heavy, important.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Your whole <radical>village</radical> - every paddy stacked on its slab of packed earth - gets loaded onto a scale. Behind it the <radical>day</radical>'s sun keeps climbing, glaring through its little window without a single cloud. The needle won't budge, because underneath it all sits one slab of <radical>ground</radical>, unmoving. The whole village is simply heavy.
items.reading_mnemonic: The ox pulling the scale, a stubborn animal named <reading>Joo</reading>, plants its hooves and refuses to shift. Villagers push and it just groans <reading>じゅう</reading>, sinking deeper into the ground instead.
items.description: 重 stacks a sun-window box (日) over the village grid (里) on top of a ground line - three pieces, tall and busy. 車 is only the simple cart shape: one box crossed top and bottom by a single line, with two wheel bars sticking out the sides - lean and symmetric where 重 is layered and heavy-looking.

example_sentences.english: This bag is really heavy.
example_sentences.furigana: このかばんはとても重[おも]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: この問題はとても重要です。
example_sentences.english: This problem is very important.
example_sentences.furigana: この問[もん]題[だい]はとても重[じゅう]要[よう]です。

items.mnemonic_text: Water (氵) breaking through a levee (夬): a decisive break.
items.meaning_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, a hiker stalls at a signpost where the path forks, a borrowed marker brush still dripping in her hand. She flicks the wet bristles — three <radical>water</radical> droplets fly off in a row and splash across the left arrow, blotting the right one out completely. Case closed: she follows whichever arrow is still legible. Decided.
items.reading_mnemonic: Perched on the signpost, a marmot named Ketch watches the paint drip and chitters <reading>けつ</reading>, <reading>Ketch</reading>, approving her choice before scrambling down the now-legible path ahead of her.

example_sentences.japanese: 会議の時間がまだ決まっていません。
example_sentences.english: The meeting time hasn't been decided yet.
example_sentences.furigana: 会[かい]議[ぎ]の時[じ]間[かん]がまだ決[き]まっていません。

example_sentences.japanese: 私が旅行の場所を決めました。
example_sentences.english: I decided on the place for the trip.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]が旅[りょ]行[こう]の場[ば]所[しょ]を決[き]めました。

example_sentences.japanese: 約束の日はもう決まりましたか。
example_sentences.english: Has the day for our appointment been decided yet?
example_sentences.furigana: 約[やく]束[そく]の日[ひ]はもう決[き]まりましたか。

items.mnemonic_text: An upright frame with pupils inside: an eye.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Look closely at this character: it's an upright frame with two pupils sitting inside it. Tip it on its side and it even looks like it's staring right back at you. That frame with pupils is exactly what it is — an <radical>eye</radical>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A woodcarver named <reading>もく</reading> is whittling a tiny wooden eye at Koichi's konbini counter, holding it up to inspect the grain. Every time he blinks, he mutters "もく, もく" as he lines the carving up with his own eye.
items.description: Count the bars inside the box. 目 is tall with two horizontals. 日 has one. 自 is 目 with a small slash added on top of the box.

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女の目は大きいです。
example_sentences.english: Her eyes are big.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]の目[め]は大[おお]きいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 祖父は目が悪いです。
example_sentences.english: My grandfather has bad eyesight.
example_sentences.furigana: 祖[そ]父[ふ]は目[め]が悪[わる]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: 自分の目で見ました。
example_sentences.english: I saw it with my own eyes.
example_sentences.furigana: 自[じ]分[ぶん]の目[め]で見[み]ました。

items.mnemonic_text: A road (辶) release (关) sending something off: to send.
items.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a delivery boy plants footstep after footstep onto the muddy road, using it to <radical>advance</radical> right up to the water's edge. He doesn't stop there — he draws his arm back and lets the parcel sail clean across, already turning to walk the same road back. Getting something moving forward until it leaves your hands entirely: that is sending.
items.reading_mnemonic: The boy's only witness is Sow, a pig who lives by the crossing, and every time he lobs a parcel over the water she gives the same unimpressed grunt, <reading>そう</reading> — which sounds exactly like someone muttering <reading>so</reading> to themselves right before they let something go.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は友達に手紙を送りました。
example_sentences.english: I sent a letter to my friend.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は友[とも]達[だち]に手[て]紙[がみ]を送[おく]りました。

example_sentences.japanese: 駅で彼を見送りました。
example_sentences.english: I saw him off at the station.
example_sentences.furigana: 駅[えき]で彼[かれ]を見[み]送[おく]りました。

example_sentences.japanese: 毎朝テレビでニュースを放送します。
example_sentences.english: Every morning, they broadcast the news on TV.
example_sentences.furigana: 毎[まい]朝[あさ]テレビでニュースを放[ほう]送[そう]します。

items.mnemonic_text: A woman (女) safe under a roof: peaceful and cheap.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a <radical>woman</radical> kneeling gracefully inside a snug little house, the <radical>roof</radical> pulled down over her like a blanket. Nothing can reach her in here — she is safe, the rent is nothing, everything is calm. A woman tucked safely under a roof is cheap and peaceful.
items.reading_mnemonic: She's spreading sweet red <reading>あん</reading> (bean paste) on a bun, humming, utterly at peace. Every bite is cheap comfort — say あん and taste that calm.
items.description: 安 means cheap or peaceful, and shows up in words for low prices, safety, and being at ease.

example_sentences.japanese: この本は安いです。
example_sentences.english: This book is cheap.
example_sentences.furigana: この本[ほん]は安[やす]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: あのレストランは安くておいしいです。
example_sentences.english: That restaurant is cheap and delicious.
example_sentences.furigana: あのレストランは安[やす]くておいしいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 昨日、安い靴を買いました。
example_sentences.english: I bought cheap shoes yesterday.
example_sentences.furigana: 昨日[きのう]、安[やす]い靴[くつ]を買[か]いました。

items.mnemonic_text: Thread (糸) running straight through the loom (圣): to pass through time.
items.meaning_mnemonic: In the temple's back room, the same <radical>right hand</radical> that keeps sneaking into the cookie jar now reaches out <radical>again</radical> and again, feeding a spool of <radical>thread</radical> through a loom staked into the <radical>earth</radical> like a signpost. Row after row, the thread passes through the frame while the monk drones the same sutra over and over, never stopping.
items.reading_mnemonic: The apprentice threading the loom is named <reading>Kay</reading>, and every time the shuttle passes through she exhales a low <reading>けい</reading>, matching the monk's chant beat for beat until the thread and the sutra finish the row together.

example_sentences.japanese: 日本に来てから一年経った。
example_sentences.english: A year has passed since I came to Japan.
example_sentences.furigana: 日本[にほん]に来[き]てから一[いち]年[ねん]経[た]った。

example_sentences.japanese: 日本の経済はとても大きい。
example_sentences.english: Japan's economy is very big.
example_sentences.furigana: 日本[にほん]の経[けい]済[ざい]はとても大[おお]きい。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は毎月経費を払う。
example_sentences.english: He pays expenses every month.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は毎[まい]月[つき]経[けい]費[ひ]を払[はら]う。

items.mnemonic_text: Thread (糸) sold (売) onward without a break: to continue.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane's shrine cat sleeps under its usual <radical>cover</radical>, tucked snug past its ears, but a stray <radical>thread</radical> from the blanket keeps unspooling down the mossy steps. It runs past a pair of <radical>human legs</radical> marching in place, refusing to stop, straight to the <radical>samurai</radical> duck on sentry duty, who salutes and lets the thread run on under his feet rather than break the line. Nothing here ends — it all just continues.
items.reading_mnemonic: At those same shrine steps, a tourist named <reading>Zach</reading> tries to leave but his legs won't quit marching in place, round and round, and every stomp echoes <reading>ぞく</reading> off the mossy stone, on and on, refusing to stop.

example_sentences.japanese: 授業はまだ続いています。
example_sentences.english: The class is still going on.
example_sentences.furigana: 授[じゅ]業[ぎょう]はまだ続[つづ]いています。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は毎日勉強を続けています。
example_sentences.english: He keeps studying every day.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は毎[まい]日[にち]勉[べん]強[きょう]を続[つづ]けています。

example_sentences.japanese: この話の続きを聞きたいです。
example_sentences.english: I want to hear the rest of this story.
example_sentences.furigana: この話[はなし]の続[つづ]きを聞[き]きたいです。

items.mnemonic_text: Bones (歹) left over after the cut (戔): what remains.
items.meaning_mnemonic: At the shrine gate, the <radical>halberd</radical> that toppled when a guard's scarf snagged its blade now lies clattered in the dirt, its shaft snapped clean at the joint — a fresh crack of <radical>death / bad luck</radical> running through the wood. Nobody hauls it away; it just stays where it fell, broken but present. Whatever's left after the disaster is what remains.
items.reading_mnemonic: Every morning the shrine's groundskeeper cat, a stubborn old tom named <reading>Zan</reading>, sniffs at the broken halberd and grumbles <reading>ざん</reading>, deciding again it isn't his job to move it — so there it stays.

example_sentences.japanese: 冷蔵庫に卵が二つ残っています。
example_sentences.english: Two eggs are left in the fridge.
example_sentences.furigana: 冷[れい]蔵[ぞう]庫[こ]に卵[たまご]が二[ふた]つ残[のこ]っています。

example_sentences.japanese: 今日は雨で残念です。
example_sentences.english: It's raining today, which is a shame.
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]は雨[あめ]で残[ざん]念[ねん]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は今日も残業です。
example_sentences.english: He has overtime again today.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は今日[きょう]も残[ざん]業[ぎょう]です。

items.mnemonic_text: Earth (土) piled ever higher (曽): to increase.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The sun climbs behind that windowed bar marking a new <radical>day</radical>, and the farmer eyes his flooded <radical>rice field</radical> creeping past the wooden signpost planted in the <radical>earth</radical> — the plots multiplying past the marker, claiming more ground than yesterday. By sundown there is simply more of everything, mud and water both. That's increase.
items.reading_mnemonic: Back at that same signpost, a farmer named Zo watches the water creep higher up the wood and grunts <reading>ぞう</reading> each time — flat and low, like saying '<reading>zo</reading>' with a shrug. By dusk he's grunted it so many times the whole field has crept higher than the post itself.

example_sentences.japanese: 体重が増えました。
example_sentences.english: My weight increased.
example_sentences.furigana: 体[たい]重[じゅう]が増[ふ]えました。

example_sentences.japanese: 図書館の本が増えました。
example_sentences.english: The library's books have increased.
example_sentences.furigana: 図[と]書[しょ]館[かん]の本[ほん]が増[ふ]えました。

example_sentences.japanese: 会社は社員を増やしました。
example_sentences.english: The company hired more staff.
example_sentences.furigana: 会[かい]社[しゃ]は社[しゃ]員[いん]を増[ふ]やしました。

items.mnemonic_text: Water (氵) cut down (咸) to less: to decrease.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The guard's <radical>halberd</radical> clatters down as a scarf yanks it off the gate, knocking over a cup — <radical>water</radical> flicks out drop by drop, like droplets off a wet brush, spattering into a waiting <radical>mouth</radical> below that gulps each one down. By the last drop the cup stands empty. That's decrease.
items.reading_mnemonic: Watching his cup drain past his open mouth, the guard groans <reading>げん</reading> between gulps — flat, like saying '<reading>gen</reading>' each time the water level drops. One groan per gulp, and there's less in the cup with every single one.

example_sentences.japanese: 最近、体重が少し減りました。
example_sentences.english: I've lost a little weight recently.
example_sentences.furigana: 最[さい]近[きん]、体[たい]重[じゅう]が少[すこ]し減[へ]りました。

example_sentences.japanese: お菓子を減らして、毎朝走っています。
example_sentences.english: I've cut back on sweets and I run every morning.
example_sentences.furigana: お菓[か]子[し]を減[へ]らして、毎[まい]朝[あさ]走[はし]っています。

example_sentences.japanese: 財布のお金がだんだん減っています。
example_sentences.english: The money in my wallet is slowly dwindling.
example_sentences.furigana: 財[さい]布[ふ]のお金[かね]がだんだん減[へ]っています。

items.mnemonic_text: A body (尸) stretching (由) out to reach: to deliver, arrive.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Guests keep stepping around the sprawled <radical>corpse / body</radical>, and nobody expects him to move for the doorbell. So when a package arrives, the courier just drags the whole box across the tatami until it bumps his outstretched leg — the only way anything ever reaches him tonight. It has been delivered.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the same party, a courier named <reading>Kai</reading> keeps sighing <reading>かい</reading> as he hauls yet another box across the tatami to the sprawled body's leg, resigned to the fact that delivery here always means dragging, never handing.

example_sentences.japanese: 昨日、母から手紙が届きました。
example_sentences.english: A letter from my mother arrived yesterday.
example_sentences.furigana: 昨日[きのう]、母[はは]から手[て]紙[がみ]が届[とど]きました。

example_sentences.japanese: この荷物を隣の部屋に届けてください。
example_sentences.english: Please take this package to the room next door.
example_sentences.furigana: この荷[に]物[もつ]を隣[となり]の部屋[へや]に届[とど]けてください。

example_sentences.japanese: 財布を無くしたので、交番に届け出ました。
example_sentences.english: I lost my wallet, so I reported it at the police box.
example_sentences.furigana: 財[さい]布[ふ]を無[な]くしたので、交[こう]番[ばん]に届[とど]け出[で]ました。

items.mnemonic_text: Words (言) sold (売) to your eyes: reading.
items.meaning_mnemonic: On the left the <radical>speech</radical> is doing its usual thing, sentence after sentence stacking up out of that little mouth. On the right the very serious armoured <radical>samurai</radical> duck has climbed down off the garden wall and planted himself on a pair of sturdy <radical>human legs</radical>, feet apart, refusing to blink. He isn't listening to a word of it — his eyes are running down the stacked lines, top to bottom, silently. That is not hearing speech. That is reading it.
items.reading_mnemonic: The reader you find hunched over those lines of speech is a poison-pen critic, and you nickname her Doku (<reading>どく</reading>) because every review she reads she then tears apart. Watch her read a page and you can practically see the どく venom drip off her pen.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は毎日本を読みます。
example_sentences.english: I read books every day.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は毎[まい]日本[にほん]を読[よ]みます。

example_sentences.japanese: 図書館で面白い雑誌を読みました。
example_sentences.english: I read an interesting magazine at the library.
example_sentences.furigana: 図[と]書[しょ]館[かん]で面[おも]白[しろ]い雑[ざっ]誌[し]を読[よ]みました。

example_sentences.japanese: 誰がその手紙を読みましたか。
example_sentences.english: Who read that letter?
example_sentences.furigana: 誰[だれ]がその手[て]紙[がみ]を読[よ]みましたか。

items.mnemonic_text: Food (食) beside a person yawning (欠) for a drink.
items.meaning_mnemonic: On the left is the radical for food and eating, and on the right is a person opening their mouth wide in a <radical>yawn</radical>, a lack. But this yawning mouth isn't tired — it's tipping a glass back, mouth wide open to gulp something down. When you see food beside that gaping, thirsty mouth, you drink.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini a regular named Inn slaps a cold can on the beeping till and says the same thing every single day: "First, I drink!" You can hear the 「<reading>いん</reading>」 right at the front of Inn's name as he cracks it open.
items.description: Means "drink"; the everyday kanji in the verb 飲む, to drink.

example_sentences.japanese: 毎朝コーヒーを飲みます。
example_sentences.english: I drink coffee every morning.
example_sentences.furigana: 毎[まい]朝[あさ]コーヒーを飲[の]みます。

example_sentences.japanese: 冷たい飲み物が欲しいです。
example_sentences.english: I want a cold drink.
example_sentences.furigana: 冷[つめ]たい飲[の]み物[もの]が欲[ほ]しいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 昨日、友達とお酒を飲みました。
example_sentences.english: I drank alcohol with my friend yesterday.
example_sentences.furigana: 昨日[きのう]、友[とも]達[だち]とお酒[さけ]を飲[の]みました。

items.mnemonic_text: Goods laid out on a stand: selling.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The very serious armoured <radical>samurai</radical> duck has abandoned the garden wall and set up a stall, balanced on a pair of sturdy <radical>human legs</radical> planted wide behind a table of stacked goods. It still refuses to blink, it refuses to come down on the price, and it shouts at everyone who slows down. A samurai on braced legs behind a loaded table has exactly one job: to sell.
items.reading_mnemonic: The vendor keeps yelling one thing at every customer who walks past: "Buy! <reading>ばい</reading>, ばい, one for you and one for the baby!" He'll sell to anyone who slows down, and every pitch ends on that same ばい.

example_sentences.japanese: 友達に自転車を売りました。
example_sentences.english: I sold my bicycle to a friend.
example_sentences.furigana: 友[とも]達[だち]に自[じ]転[てん]車[しゃ]を売[う]りました。

example_sentences.japanese: デパートで服を売っています。
example_sentences.english: They sell clothes at the department store.
example_sentences.furigana: デパートで服[ふく]を売[う]っています。

example_sentences.japanese: その車は売りません。
example_sentences.english: I will not sell that car.
example_sentences.furigana: その車[くるま]は売[う]りません。

items.mnemonic_text: Flowing long hair on an elder: long and the eldest.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Look at the whole character: it's an old man standing side-on, with a flowing beard and long hair streaming down past his shoulders, and a walking stick planted at the bottom. He's the eldest, the one everyone else follows — so this is your picture of something <radical>long</radical>, and of the elder who leads.
items.reading_mnemonic: That long-bearded elder is the leader of a whole troupe of butterflies, and he lets one land on his flowing hair — a <reading>ちょう</reading> (butterfly). Every time you see this kanji, picture the ちょう resting on the leader's long locks.
items.description: Means long or leader; shows up in words for length, seniority, and being the head of something, like a school principal or a company chief.

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女の髪は長いです。
example_sentences.english: Her hair is long.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]の髪[かみ]は長[なが]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: 私は長い手紙を書きました。
example_sentences.english: I wrote a long letter.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は長[なが]い手[て]紙[がみ]を書[か]きました。

example_sentences.japanese: 先生の話は長いです。
example_sentences.english: The teacher's stories are long.
example_sentences.furigana: 先[せん]生[せい]の話[はなし]は長[なが]いです。

items.mnemonic_text: A flexed arm pushing: power and strength.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Look at this single stroke and picture a bent arm flexing hard — the elbow cocked, the muscle bulging. That one flexed arm is all you need to see: it's pure <radical>power</radical>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A weightlifter named Rio steps up to the bar and gives a warrior's yell as she flexes: "<reading>りょく</reading>!" The whole gym feels the raw strength in that shout.
items.description: 力 and 九 are both two strokes with a hook, and the hooks point opposite ways. 力 starts with a flat horizontal that turns down and hooks to the left, with a slash cutting through it. 九 starts with a short slash, then a stroke that curves right and flicks upward.

example_sentences.japanese: あの男の人は力が強いですね。
example_sentences.english: That man is strong, isn't he?
example_sentences.furigana: あの男[おとこ]の人[ひと]は力[ちから]が強[つよ]いですね。

example_sentences.japanese: 私の祖父は力が弱いです。
example_sentences.english: My grandfather doesn't have much strength.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]の祖[そ]父[ふ]は力[ちから]が弱[よわ]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: テーブルが重いですから、一緒に力を使いましょう。
example_sentences.english: The table is heavy, so let's use our strength together.
example_sentences.furigana: テーブルが重[おも]いですから、一[いっ]緒[しょ]に力[ちから]を使[つか]いましょう。

items.mnemonic_text: The sun (日) already up over the ground (十): early.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Someone has scratched the <radical>ten</radical> mark into the dirt — two matchsticks crossed, the tally you cut when you've counted both hands — and stood it upright like a fencepost. Behind it the <radical>sun</radical>, that window with a bar in it, comes climbing up to start a new <radical>day</radical> and clears the top of the post before you've counted anywhere near ten. It's up hours ahead of your alarm, and now everything you do today has to be fast: early, fast.
items.reading_mnemonic: There's a rooster at Grandma Kane's shrine who crows the moment the sun peeks over the mossy steps, way too early: "<reading>そう</reading>! そう!" he screams, so loud the cats scatter. Now you're up before dawn whether you like it or not.
items.description: Means "early" or "fast," and shows up in everyday words about time and speed like 早い (early/fast) and 早く (quickly).

example_sentences.japanese: 今日は早く起きました。
example_sentences.english: I woke up early today.
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]は早[はや]く起[お]きました。

example_sentences.japanese: 明日は早いから、寝ます。
example_sentences.english: I have an early start tomorrow, so I'm going to sleep.
example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]は早[はや]いから、寝[ね]ます。

example_sentences.japanese: 毎日早く学校へ行きます。
example_sentences.english: I go to school early every day.
example_sentences.furigana: 毎[まい]日[にち]早[はや]く学[がっ]校[こう]へ行[い]きます。

items.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>Words</radical> stand on the left, and on the right an <radical>old bird</radical> with its head cocked, waiting. You have been talking for ten minutes and the bird still cannot work out which person you mean. It hops in closer and asks the only question you have left it: <radical>who</radical>?
items.reading_mnemonic: Sui is the owl who works the gate. She leans down, blinks once, and hoots 「<reading>すい</reading>」, which in owl means name, please. Nobody gets past her without answering it. すい, すい, until you say who you are.
